dimensions.detail: Each conversation is a list of alternating user/assistant messages. For every turn the client sends messages[:turn] to /v1/chat/completions (streaming by default), so history grows turn by turn. --max-turns caps the number of MESSAGES per conversation, user and assistant counted together (e.g. 2, 4, 6), not user turns. Input is either a synthetic generator config (filetype=generate_conversations, where num_turns follows a distribution) or ShareGPT converted to OpenAI message format.

After every turn, send_turn overwrites the dataset's assistant message with the text the server actually streamed back, or appends it if the dataset has no answer, so the next turn's history holds real responses. In synthetic mode the dataset assistant text is filler that only sets max_tokens; min_tokens is commented out. --verify-output compares the real answer with the dataset answer. -o writes out the conversations with the server's answers. Warmup-step answers to turn 1 are also real and carry into the main run.

The synthetic config has two prefix options. common_prefix_num_tokens (optional) is one prefix shared by all conversations; its length is sampled once. prefix_num_tokens is a unique prefix per conversation, drawn from constant/uniform/lognormal/zipf/poisson. Missing: (1) the pool size is fixed at 1, so there is no way to have K distinct shared personas; (2) the prefix is prepended to the first USER message, not sent as a system-role message; (3) system messages are not supported at all. The ShareGPT converter rejects conversations that do not strictly alternate user/assistant. send_turn asserts that the message being sent is role=user, so a leading system message fails the assertion on turn 1. The prefix only reaches later turns because it is part of the history.

There is a zipf distribution (np.random.zipf with alpha and an optional max), but it only samples numeric fields such as num_turns and token counts. It cannot pick which shared prefix a session uses, because there is only one common prefix, sampled once. The only way around this is to generate a conversations list offline with persona text already baked into the first user messages; the tool itself does nothing here. Grepped zipf/popular/skew/weight in benchmarks/multi_turn: the only zipf hits are the numeric Distribution class, its parser and the README.

The only delay is --request-rate, a per-client rate. After every request, successful or not, the client sleeps np.random.exponential(1/rate); the default 0 means no sleep. By default -k (--max-active-conversations) equals -p (--num-clients), so each client has exactly one active conversation. In that case the sleep acts as an exponential think time between consecutive turns of one conversation (mean 1/rate). It also applies between one conversation's last turn and the next conversation's first turn. With -k above -p, each client interleaves several conversations (--conversation-sampling round_robin|random). The gap between one conversation's turns then also includes the other conversations' latencies and sleeps. Missing: a think-time setting separate from the rate and scoped to the session; any distribution other than exponential; per-conversation settings. With -v, the actual gap is reported afterwards as time_between_user_turns_sec (measured, not configured). Open PR #43212 fixes the sleep so it matches the configured rate. Open PR #43217 only adds an exponential option to the dataset numeric distributions, not to think time.

Load is closed-loop, with no arrival process for session starts. main_mp puts every conversation into a shared multiprocessing Queue at startup. A client pulls a new conversation whenever it has fewer than max_active_conversations/num_clients active ones. The only Poisson process is the per-client, per-request sleep described under think_time. Grepped poisson/arrival/session: no scheduling of session starts found.

Concurrency is fixed: -p/--num-clients starts N processes, and each keeps at most one request in flight (sequential awaits), so concurrency is N. -k/--max-active-conversations is split evenly per client. -n/--max-num-requests caps the total, divided per client. By default the run stops as soon as any client finishes (--no-early-stop disables that). Missing: multiple load stages or a sweep in one run with per-stage aggregation, and a duration-based stop (--max-duration-sec is open PR #43215).

--warmup-step first sends turn 1 of every conversation, with one active conversation per client and max_turns=1. The main run then skips that turn (skip_first_turn), and its samples are left out. Alternatively, --warmup-percentages (e.g. 0%,50%) drops the first X% of samples by start time and prints a summary for each percentage; it is only parsed when --warmup-step is not set. Warmup is by sample count or first turn, never by time.

Reports three values per request. ttft_ms is measured at the first non-empty content delta and adjusted when the first chunk holds several tokens. tpot_ms = (latency - ttft) / (output tokens - first-chunk tokens), with tokens counted by the client tokenizer. latency_ms is E2E. Per-chunk gaps are collected in send_request and averaged into ServerResponse.tpot_ms, but send_turn throws that value away. Percentiles come from pandas describe: mean/std/min/max plus p25/50/75/90, adding p99 at 100 or more samples, p99.9 at 1000 and p99.99 at 10000. Missing: p95 (the list is hard-coded), and any ITL distribution (no token- or chunk-level ITL percentiles).

Requests explicitly send stream_options.include_usage=false. Input and output token counts come from a local HF AutoTokenizer loaded from --model, which must be a loadable tokenizer path. It is applied to message contents without the chat template. Server usage is never read.

The only related output is approx_cached_percent = client-tokenized history tokens / input tokens. It is a workload property: an upper bound that assumes the whole history is cached, and it is the same whether or not the server caches anything. It is not a measured hit rate. It appears in per-request RequestStats (printed with --print-content, exported with --stats-json-output) but is dropped from the printed summary and Excel tables (exclude list). Grepped cached_tokens, prompt_tokens_details, prometheus and /metrics in benchmarks/multi_turn: 0 hits. Neither server usage nor server metrics are read.
Grepped goodput and slo in benchmarks/multi_turn/*.py: 0 hits. process_statistics prints only runtime, requests/sec and describe() tables.
Grepped cost, price, dollar and gpu in benchmarks/multi_turn/*.py: 0 hits. The summary reports only runtime_sec and requests_per_sec.

Grepped prometheus and /metrics: 0 hits. The only live output is a periodic log line (DebugStats moving averages plus estimated req/s). The only server queries are GET /version and GET /v1/models at startup.

--seed (default 0) seeds random and np.random in the main process, so synthetic conversations are deterministic: turn counts, token lengths and text offsets. Each client process reseeds with seed+client_id+1, which drives its exponential sleeps and random conversation choice. Missing: conversations reach clients through a shared multiprocessing Queue that all clients read concurrently, so which client gets which conversation is racy. The delays and interleaving around a given conversation are therefore not reproducible. Real server responses also change the contexts of later turns.

Planned and actual send times are never compared (there is no planned schedule, only post-request sleeps), and client overload never triggers a warning. Grepped lag, behind, late, overload and schedule: nothing relevant. Progress logs show only estimated req/s and remaining runtime. Client-side tokenization of every request and response in the hot path is a likely client bottleneck, and it goes unreported.

tools.notes: The closest match to personaload in vLLM. It is a standalone script, not part of the vllm CLI, with its own requirements.txt (numpy, pandas, aiohttp, transformers, xlsxwriter, tqdm), and it needs a locally loadable HF tokenizer. The README title makes the design goal clear: benchmarking KV-cache offloading, not character chat. Other features: an optional non-standard conversation_id body field plus X-Session-ID header (--send-conversation-id); --api-key/--header; retries with exponential backoff (--max-retries, timeouts only); Excel (-e) and per-request JSON (--stats-json-output) export. TTFT ignores chunks without content (such as reasoning deltas); reasoning mode is open PR #43739. Open, unmerged PRs signal known gaps (all verified OPEN via gh): #53075 (asyncio v2 to fix a deadlock), #57181 (drain active conversations), #43212 (sleep does not match the configured rate), #43215 (--max-duration-sec), #42575 (extra request body), #43739 (reasoning mode), #43217 (exponential dataset distribution). Gaps relative to personaload: no system-role persona pool, no Zipf persona choice, no session-level Poisson arrival, no stages, no server usage or cached_tokens, no SLO, cost or Prometheus output.

dimensions.detail: Every SampleRequest is independent and single-shot. The ShareGPT, HF ConversationDataset (ShareGPT/Vicuna) and MT-Bench loaders take only the first user turn (conversations[0], or turns[0]) as the prompt, plus conversations[1] for the output length. The chat backend passes a pre-built messages list through when a dataset sets chat_messages or the prompt is already a list of role/content dicts. Only the BFCL loader uses this, and only for the first turn ('skip multi-turn categories'). CustomDataset chat-templates the prompt into a string, so pre-baked histories cannot be supplied. Grepped multi_turn, multi-turn, conversation, history and session under vllm/benchmarks: no multi-turn session logic.

Does not apply, since there is no multi-turn. generated_text is collected only as the fallback for counting output tokens and for the saved result JSON (generated_texts), and is never fed back as context.

--dataset-name prefix_repetition sets the number of distinct prefixes with --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes (default 10), plus fixed (not distributed) --prefix-repetition-prefix-len, --prefix-repetition-suffix-len and --prefix-repetition-output-len. Prefixes are random-token text, and each gets num_requests // num_prefixes prompts. --dataset-name random has --random-prefix-len: one prefix, generated once and shared by all requests. --dataset-name timed_trace rebuilds arbitrary prefix sharing from a trace's hash_ids (each hash ID maps to a deterministic chunk of tokens), but it needs a completions backend (pre-tokenized prompts), not chat. Missing: the prefix is always part of one user message, never a system-role message, and it is not reused across a session's growing history. Correction: the MLPerf HF loader builds [system, user] but renders it with tokenizer.apply_chat_template(tokenize=False) into a single string prompt. The openai-chat backend then wraps that string in one role=user message, so no system-role message goes over the wire.

Every prefix in prefix_repetition gets exactly num_requests // num_prefixes prompts, a uniform split, before random.shuffle. A hand-crafted timed_trace whose hash_ids follow a Zipf distribution could encode skew, but that path is completions-only and has no generator. Grepped zipf, skew, popular and weight in vllm/benchmarks: 0 zipf hits.

There are no sessions, so there is no delay between turns. The only timing control is the per-request inter-arrival schedule in get_request. Grepped think, delay and sleep: only arrival-schedule sleeps, plus the fixed interval of the probe loop.

Arrival is per request only. --request-rate (default inf = everything at t=0) with --burstiness uses a gamma inter-arrival: burstiness=1 is Poisson, and burstiness=inf gives fixed intervals. The delays are precomputed and rescaled so the total matches num_prompts/rate. --dataset-name timed_trace (self-timed by default) replays per-request timestamps, completions backend only. None of these work at session level.

--max-concurrency adds an asyncio.Semaphore; with --request-rate inf this is a fixed-concurrency closed loop. --ramp-up-strategy linear|exponential with --ramp-up-start-rps and --ramp-up-end-rps changes the rate within one run and records rps_change_events timestamps. Missing: metrics are aggregated over the whole run only, with no per-stage aggregation. Multiple stages need `vllm bench sweep serve`, which runs separate processes (see that entry). --probe-request-rate adds side-channel probe requests that bypass the concurrency semaphore.

--num-warmups N sends N copies of input_requests[0] (the readiness-test prompt) under the same concurrency limit before the main run, and excludes them from metrics. Missing: warmup is count-based on one identical prompt, which primes the prefix cache only for that prompt. There is no time-based warmup period of representative traffic.

Reports TTFT, TPOT, ITL and E2EL, each with mean/median/std, plus any list of percentiles via --metric-percentiles (e.g. 50,90,95,99; default 99 only). --percentile-metrics selects metrics; the default for generation is ttft,tpot,itl, so e2el must be added. Other options: client_queue_time and e2el_including_client_queue. Caveats: ITL is the gap between SSE chunks, not true per-token ITL, unless the server streams one token per chunk. TTFT is taken at the first chunk with a non-empty choices array, which may be a role-only or reasoning delta with no content. TTFT/TPOT/ITL are printed only when a tokenizer is loaded; with --skip-tokenizer-init only E2EL is printed. Also reported: peak output tokens/s, peak concurrent requests, and an optional --plot-timeline HTML.

The openai-chat backend sends stream_options.include_usage=true. The final usage chunk sets output_tokens = usage.completion_tokens and overwrites prompt_len with usage.prompt_tokens. Fallback: if output_tokens is missing or 0, calculate_metrics re-tokenizes generated_text with the client tokenizer, or counts 1 when --skip-tokenizer-init is set. A client tokenizer is still loaded by default, for dataset construction.

The usage parser reads only completion_tokens and prompt_tokens; prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens is ignored. The server's /metrics is scraped before and after the run only for spec-decode and diffusion counters, not prefix-cache hits. Grepped cached_tokens, prompt_tokens_details, prefix_cache, cache_hit and hit_rate in vllm/benchmarks: the only hit is sweep/server.py's /reset_prefix_cache.

--goodput takes KEY:VALUE pairs in ms with keys ttft, tpot or e2el. A request counts as good only if it meets every given SLO. request_goodput (good requests per second) is printed as 'Request goodput (req/s)' and saved to the JSON. Missing for personaload: no run-level pass/fail verdict on percentile SLOs, and no good-request ratio is printed (derive it as goodput / request_throughput). The separate script benchmarks/auto_tune/auto_tune.sh wraps vllm bench serve and applies a run-level pass/fail on P99 E2EL.
Grepped cost, price, dollar, usd and gpu_hour in vllm/benchmarks: no hits. The result JSON has throughput but no cost.
The tool does not expose a Prometheus endpoint. It only scrapes the server's /metrics before and after the run, for speculative-decoding and diffusion deltas. Live feedback is a tqdm progress bar.

--seed (default 0) is passed as random_seed to the dataset constructors; RandomDataset uses np.random.default_rng(seed). main_async also seeds random and np.random, so the precomputed gamma/Poisson inter-arrival schedule and random LoRA assignment are deterministic. The same seed gives the same prompts and the same send schedule for the random, prefix_repetition, sharegpt and HF datasets. Caveat: timed_trace is built with TimedTrace(**vars(args)), so --seed never reaches random_seed. Its prompt tokens are also seeded from Python's per-process-salted hash(), so its content is not reproducible across runs unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed. That path is completions-only.

The tool records client_queue_time: the time from when the arrival generator releases a request (just before asyncio.create_task) to when request_func actually starts. That covers the wait on the --max-concurrency semaphore plus event-loop delay before the task first runs. Per-request queue_times are always saved in the result JSON. Percentiles are printed only when --max-concurrency is set; E2EL including the client queue is printed only when the request rate is also finite. Missing: get_request sleeps toward the absolute delay_ts schedule but never records how late the generator itself is. Nothing warns when the client falls behind schedule, and there is no CPU or saturation check. freeze_gc_heap() is called to reduce GC pauses.

tools.notes: Values accepted by --dataset-name: sharegpt, burstgpt, sonnet, random (default), random-mm, random-rerank, hf, custom (JSONL with a prompt field, chat-templated into a string unless --skip-chat-template), custom_audio, custom_image, prefix_repetition, spec_bench, speed_bench, timed_trace. timed_trace replays timestamped traces with Mooncake-style hash_ids; it is self-timed by default and needs the vllm/openai completions backend. hf routes to many HF loaders: ShareGPT/Vicuna conversations, VisionArena, MMVU, InstructCoder, MT-Bench (first turn only), HumanEval, GSM8K, AIMO, BFCL (first turn only), MLPerf, ASR, MMStar and more. Traffic controls: --request-rate, --burstiness (gamma), --max-concurrency, --ramp-up-strategy/--ramp-up-start-rps/--ramp-up-end-rps, --probe-request-rate, --num-warmups, --goodput, --ready-check-timeout-sec. Results: --save-result/--save-detailed JSON (per-request ttfts, itls, texts, queue_times), a PyTorch benchmark-format file, and --plot-timeline. For the random and prefix_repetition datasets, prompts are re-aligned to the server tokenizer through the vLLM-specific /tokenize and /detokenize endpoints. Use --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions for chat. Random datasets default to ignore_eos. Related: benchmarks/auto_tune/auto_tune.sh wraps vllm bench serve. It sweeps server configs, steps the request rate down until P99 E2EL meets MAX_LATENCY_ALLOWED_MS, and models a cache-hit percentage with --random-prefix-len. vllm bench serve is a strong single-turn OpenAI-compatible SSE benchmark, but it has no sessions, history, think time, cached-token reporting, cost or live metrics.

`sweep serve` runs the Cartesian product of the --serve-params and --bench-params JSON files (each a list of dicts, or a dict of named dicts), e.g. max_concurrency or request_rate lists. --link-vars filters combinations, and --num-runs repeats each one (default 3). It writes per-run JSON, per-combination summary.json and a combined summary.csv. `sweep serve_workload` (--workload-var request_rate|max_concurrency, --workload-iters) first measures a serial run (max_concurrency=1) and a batch run (max_concurrency=num_prompts), then sweeps evenly spaced values in between. Caveats: each stage is a separate `vllm bench serve` subprocess, not a stage inside one continuous run. --serve-cmd is REQUIRED: the sweep always launches the server itself, once per serve-params combination, as a subprocess. It then polls /health on the host/port parsed from serve-cmd (default localhost:8000) and fails if that process exits. Benchmarking an external or remote OpenAI-compatible server therefore needs a dummy long-running serve-cmd plus --after-bench-cmd.
